<reason>PRO built a concrete causal story (coached test scores, legacy/athletic tilts, unpaid internships, financial cushions sorting the already-qualified) and then converted CON's own core distinction—class shapes who develops ability, institutions select the developed ability—into a concession that the pipeline reproduces class end to end. CON's defense was almost entirely a burden argument ("PRO shows advantage exists, not that merit is overstated or privilege underadmitted") without ever offering a positive picture of how much class actually contributes or evidence that successful people acknowledge it adequately; its Q1 answer (need-based aid, wider recruitment) was thin against PRO's point that exceptions don't explain how most arrived. CON did score real hits—PRO's "class decides who becomes partner" was overstated and the "admit" half rests on characterizing narratives rather than evidence—but PRO answered both pressure questions directly and sharply (post-floor mechanisms; "a standard nobody can fail"), and its closing crystallized the comparison CON claimed was missing: the story meritocracy tells versus the machinery CON described. PRO's clipped opening is a minor execution cost; both sides kept epistemic discipline. A clear but competitive win for PRO.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's seizure of [B1.3] in [A2.1]–[A2.2] and its follow-through in [A4.3]/[A5.1]: reframing CON's "unfair on development, meritocratic on selection" distinction as a concession that inherited preparation is simply certified by a fair-looking exam. CON's reply that reproduction of advantage doesn't equal overstatement kept the burden clash alive but never neutralized the point, and CON's Q1 answer in [B4.1] conceded that a pathway recruiting mostly affluent candidates "can reproduce advantage."</best_rebuttal>
